scenes.heading: Rechargeable batteries
scenes.sub: Two cells in one: galvanic and electrolytic
scenes.say: Your phone, your laptop and the battery in a petrol car can all be recharged hundreds of times. A rechargeable battery is really two cells in one. Let's see how.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Rolling down a ramp is free; carrying the board back up takes effort
scenes.science: Discharging is spontaneous; recharging needs a power supply
scenes.breaks: walking back up gets you exactly where you started, but each real cycle causes a little irreversible change.
scenes.say: Rolling down a skate ramp happens on its own. That's discharging: a galvanic cell turning chemical energy into electrical energy. To go again, you carry the board back up. That's recharging: a power supply forces the reverse reaction, making it an electrolytic cell.

scenes.heading: Signs stay, names swap
points: Oxidation is always at the anode
scenes.say: Here's the big idea: signs stay, names swap. Each electrode keeps its plus or minus, but every reaction reverses, so anode and cathode swap names. Oxidation is still always at the anode. Connect the charger plus to plus, minus to minus, at a higher voltage than the cell.

scenes.heading: The lead–acid battery
points: About 2 V per cell; six cells = 12 V
It stays put, so it can be turned back
scenes.say: A car's lead-acid battery has a lead negative electrode, a lead oxide positive electrode and sulfuric acid. Each cell gives about two volts, and six make twelve. On discharge, solid lead sulfate forms on both electrodes and stays put, so it can be turned back on recharge.

scenes.heading: The lithium-ion battery
scenes.say: Lithium-ion batteries are like a rocking chair. Lithium ions move out of the graphite during discharge and back in during recharge, through a non-aqueous electrolyte, because lithium reacts with water. Lithium is light and gives a high voltage, around three point seven volts.
scenes.caption: Lithium-ion batteries are like a rocking chair. Li⁺ ions move out of the graphite during discharge and back in during recharge, through a non-aqueous electrolyte, because lithium reacts with water. Lithium is light and gives a high voltage, around 3.7 V.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: A lead–acid battery is recharged at 5.00 A for 2.00 hours. What mass of lead forms? (PbSO₄ + 2e⁻ → Pb + SO₄²⁻)
scenes.say: Seventy-two hundred seconds at five amps is thirty-six thousand coulombs, or zero point three seven three one moles of electrons. Two electrons make one lead atom, so halve it, then multiply by two hundred and seven point two. That's thirty-eight point six grams.
scenes.caption: 7200 s at 5.00 A is 3.60 × 10⁴ C, or 0.3731 mol of electrons. Two electrons make one lead atom, so halve it, then multiply by 207.2. That's 38.6 g.

scenes.heading: Why batteries wear out
scenes.say: No battery lasts forever. Remember side, shape, heat, habits: side reactions, physical changes to the electrodes, extreme temperatures, and habits like overcharging, fast charging or deep discharging.

points: Products must stay on the electrodes
Li⁺ rocks between graphite and CoO₂
scenes.say: Quick recap. Discharging is galvanic, and recharging is electrolytic. Signs stay, names swap. Rechargeable cells work because their products stay on the electrodes. Now try the practice questions!
